description: I'm a Mechatronics Engineer from Peru who loves space. I visited Peru's space agency as part of a rocket project and use AI to analyze data. I grew up in the southern Andes, high and dry places that look a lot like the Moon and Mars, so this challenge feels personal. I'd like to find those places on Earth using satellite images and maps. Looking for teammates who enjoy maps, design, storytelling or web development.
summary: Before astronauts live on the Moon or Mars, their equipment and procedures must be rehearsed on Earth, yet analog sites are still chosen mostly by tradition. Puka Killajina is a deep-learning atlas that searches the whole planet for them. We trained a mode on 94957 landscapes of the Moon, Mars and Earth, taken form NASA LOLA and MOLA altimetry and global Earth relief at one common scale, so it learns to compare terrain across the three worlds. For 28 candidate Moon-base and Mars landing sites, it ranks 45599 Earth landscapes by terrain similarity, then uses NASA POWER climate data to score dryness, cold, day-night temperature swing and air pressure, stating where each analogy holds and where it breaks down. For 17 of the 28 sites it independently placed an established analog site, such as the Atacama for Jezero crater, among Earth's top 1% of matches, and 22 of its best matches are new candidates, form the Sahara to Tibet. On our web page, a mission team enters what an experiment requires and receives the matching places on Earth.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Puka Killajina takes any candidate Moon-base or Mars landing site and returns the places on Earth that resemble it most in terrain and climate, with a clear statement of where the analogy holds and where it breaks down.

HOW IT WORKS

1. We cut 94957 elevation windows of identical size (137 km wide, 1.9 km per pixel) from NASA LOLA (Moon), NASA MOLA (Mars) and NOAA ETOPO 2022 (Earth), so all three worlds are compared at the same physical scale.

2. A compact ResNet encoder learns terrain without labels, through contrastive learning: two views of the same landscape must be close, different landscapes far apart.

3. For 28 target sites, the model ranks 45599 Earth landscapes by terrain similarity. NASA POWER climate data for each one (temperature, day-night range, rainfall, pressure, humidity, wind, sunlight) is converted into transparent fidelity scores, and the best terrain matches are re-ranked with climate.

4. 38 established analog sites were never shown to the model and are used only to test it.

RESULTS

The model recognises the same landscape among 6000 others 93.1% of the time, against 62.0% for handcrafted terrain statistics. For 17 of 28 targets, an established analog site appears in Earth's top 1% of matches, and 22 of the 28 best matches are new candidates more than 300 km from any established site. Examples: Jezero crater matches the Atacama in Chile, Taurus-Littrow matches the Bolivian Altiplano, and Utopia Planitia matches the New Valley of Egypt.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Mission teams get a systematic, global and explainable shortlist of rehearsal sites instead of choosing by tradition. On the web page, a scientist or trainer enters what an experiment needs (destination, rainfall, coldest month, air pressure, sunlight, wind) and receives the matching places on a map, with guidance on what to rehearse there and what the site cannot stand in for.

TOOLS

Python, PyTorch, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, OpenCV, Plotly and FFmpeg, trained on a standard laptop. The web page is HTML, CSS and JavaScript hosted on GitHub Pages.

CREATIVITY

Instead of comparing sites by hand, one model learns a common language of terrain for three worlds. It rediscovers classic analog regions on its own and proposes new ones, from the Sahara to Tibet.

FACTORS CONSIDERED

Fair comparison (one scale and one map projection for all worlds); honesty (terrain and climate scores are kept separate, and limits such as gravity, vacuum and radiation are shown for every site); reproducibility (only open data, with all code public).
